muc.title: Who can see color?
muc.text: Radar knows something is ahead and LiDAR knows its shape, but neither knows whether the light is red or green. Only a camera can see color and text.

muc.title: An image is just numbers
muc.text: A camera also works in three steps. Step one: an 8-megapixel image is 24 million numbers, three per pixel for red, green and blue, 30 frames every second.

muc.title: AI learns to recognize things
muc.text: Step two: computer vision AI learns from millions of images where people have already marked the lights, signs and pedestrians. Once trained, it draws a box around each object with a confidence score.

muc.title: Two eyes judge distance
muc.text: Step three is judging distance. One camera can't do it, so the car uses two cameras set apart, like a pair of human eyes. The closer an object is, the more its position differs between the two images, and measuring that difference gives the distance.

muc.title: The farther, the less accurate
muc.text: The catch is that distant objects shift by only a few pixels. At 15 meters, one pixel of error is about 1 meter off, but at 60 meters it's already 15 meters off.

muc.title: Easy to trick
muc.text: Cameras also struggle in the dark and against the sun. In 2020, researchers stuck a strip of tape on a 35 mph sign, and the camera in an older car model read it as 85.

muc.title: Try losing one eye
muc.text: Close one eye and try touching two pen tips together: it's much harder. Then open Google Lens or Live Text on iPhone and point it at a sign to watch AI read the text.
